verdicts.message: No artifact signing: No artifact signing found in CI — sign your released artifacts with whatever your ecosystem ships (`cosign sign` over the image digest your pipeline pushes, so a consumer can `cosign verify` what they pull, cosign/sigstore for container images) so consumers can verify what you built. What was searched, so you can tell an absence from a miss: this repository's CI files, the scripts they invoke and its own composite actions, its root build manifest and its release manifest, its release task runner if it has one, and its own release automation script — plus the trusted-publishing declarations that sign on the registry's side. A signature produced by a pipeline whose configuration is not in this repository, or by a signer whose name is none of the ones this check carries, is not seen here.
verdicts.reason: The release pushed the image with an unsigned BuildKit provenance; nothing a consumer could verify.
verdicts.action: repository fixed in the scripted history: signed build-provenance attestation pushed to the registry, verified by the deploy workflow (sprint 3, 2026-09-04)

verdicts.message: Low IaC: DS-0026: No HEALTHCHECK defined. Add HEALTHCHECK instruction in your Dockerfile. Add HEALTHCHECK instruction in Dockerfile. Without one the runtime only knows whether the process is alive, not whether it is serving, so a wedged container is restarted by nobody. The step: add a `HEALTHCHECK` to the image that probes the service the way a client would — this image already declares `EXPOSE 8080`, so a request to `localhost:8080` on the service's own health or root route, exiting non-zero when it does not answer, is the probe — and give it an `--interval`, a `--timeout` and a `--start-period` long enough to cover startup. If the image ships no HTTP client, probe with whatever the runtime already has, or declare the check in the orchestrator instead and say so here.
verdicts.reason: No HEALTHCHECK on a Kubernetes-only image; probes are in the manifest.

verdicts.message: No AppArmor/SELinux confinement: Workloads declare no AppArmor or SELinux profile. A mandatory-access-control profile confines what a compromised container can touch on the host, complementing seccomp's syscall filter.
verdicts.reason: seccomp RuntimeDefault and dropped capabilities are set; AppArmor/SELinux is a further hardening step.

verdicts.message: No runtime threat detection: No runtime threat-detection engine (Tetragon TracingPolicy / Falco) is committed. These observe process, file and network activity in-kernel and can alert or kill on malicious behaviour a static scan cannot catch.
verdicts.reason: Runtime threat detection is a cluster platform concern.

verdicts.message: No named authorization policies: Authorization IS enforced here (by route guards, auth middleware or checks that refuse a caller) — this is NOT a claim that endpoints are unprotected. What's missing is a NAMED rule set: who may do what is encoded inline where it is checked, so the rules can't be listed, reviewed or tested apart from the code that applies them. Recommendation, not a defect.
verdicts.reason: The row itself says authorization is enforced; the scope pre-handlers per route are the named rule set (ADR 0002).

falseNegatives.reason: GET /api/dispatch/drivers/available (dispatch-routes.ts:73-96) is registered without the authenticate and requireScope pre-handlers that every other /api route has; it calls dispatch with the gateway's service token and relays the driver roster to anonymous callers. No rule models route-level authorization in Fastify; C2 reports only the absence of 'named' policies and says authorization is enforced.

upstream-client.ts:88-109 logs `request: { method, url, headers }` on every upstream failure; the headers include `authorization: Bearer <service token>`, which the pino redaction list (req.headers.authorization only) does not cover. The credential/personal-data-in-log rules do not read fields of a logged object (same blind spot as bench-ts-security-injection PII-001).

observations: Recall 0/2 on a Fastify BFF: neither the unauthenticated route nor the token in the failure log is seen; both are integration-level defects (authorization boundary, credential leak) that need route-registration and object-field analysis.
Trap resistance 6/7 contained (TRP-006 DS-0026 caught); in the model pass TRP-007 (D20 on ADR 0001) caught.
